stem: A nurse teaches a client how to use a newly prescribed antibiotic safely. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.A: I will take the antibiotic exactly as prescribed, will not share it or save leftover doses for another illness, and will contact my healthcare professional if I have questions or adverse effects.
options.B: I should stop the antibiotic on my own as soon as I feel better, even if the prescription instructions say to continue it.
options.C: I can save unused antibiotics for the next time I develop similar symptoms because this reduces unnecessary clinic visits.
options.D: If a family member develops similar symptoms, sharing my antibiotic is appropriate as long as we take the same dose.

rationale: A is correct. CDC's current antibiotic-use guidance advises clients to take antibiotics exactly as prescribed, not share them, not save them for later, and discuss questions or side effects with a healthcare professional. This wording is more accurate than a blanket instruction to 'finish every course no matter what,' because the prescribed duration itself may be changed by the treating clinician when clinically appropriate. B substitutes the client's own decision for the prescription. C and D can delay correct diagnosis and expose others to ineffective or harmful treatment.
educational_objective: Teach clients to use antibiotics exactly as prescribed, avoid sharing or saving leftover antibiotics, and seek professional guidance rather than independently shortening, extending, or reusing antimicrobial therapy.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts; Antibiotic Use and Antimicrobial Resistance Facts
source_version_date: Healthy Habits dated September 23, 2025; current CDC antibiotic-use resources accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Healthy Habits — 'Take antibiotics exactly as prescribed': take them exactly as prescribed; do not share antibiotics; do not save them for later; do not take antibiotics prescribed for someone else; contact a healthcare professional with questions. Antibiotic Use and Antimicrobial Resistance Facts — misuse includes taking the wrong antibiotic, wrong dose, or antibiotic for the wrong length of time; appropriate use is necessary to reduce harm and antimicrobial-resistance pressure.
source_claim_supported: Safe patient-level antibiotic stewardship means taking antibiotics according to current prescription instructions, not sharing or saving them, and involving the healthcare professional in treatment changes rather than self-modifying therapy.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: provide health teaching that supports appropriate medication use, prevention of infection, and risk-reducing health behaviors.
blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — patient antibiotic-use education
correction_summary: Rebuilt the raw stewardship item to remove the outdated blanket phrase 'complete the full prescribed course.' Current CDC guidance uses 'take antibiotics exactly as prescribed,' which preserves clinician-directed duration changes while still preventing self-discontinuation, sharing, or reuse of leftovers.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against CDC's September 2025 antibiotic Do's and Don'ts and current 2026 antibiotic-use resources.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A reproduces current CDC patient instructions. B creates unsupervised early discontinuation. C and D promote reuse/sharing specifically discouraged by CDC.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; exactly-as-prescribed use with no sharing/saving.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; the client should not independently alter duration.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; antibiotics should not be saved for future illness.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; antibiotics should not be shared.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A preserves both adherence and clinician-directed flexibility. No option relies on the obsolete universal 'finish the course regardless of updated instructions' formulation.
audit_findings.cueing: All options describe realistic patient antibiotic-use behaviors.
audit_findings.blueprint: Preventive medication-use education fits Health Promotion and Maintenance.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked the modern stewardship debate around fixed-course completion. The final item follows CDC's exact-as-prescribed wording and does not tell clients to self-stop early or override clinician instructions. No second answer remained.
